summary: Describes standard programming interfaces for the Service Location Protocol in C and Java, so applications can discover services in a consistent way. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: The Service Location Protocol lets a program ask the network what services are available instead of being told in advance. This memo defines the programming interface to that protocol for two languages, C and Java, and two file formats that let a machine be configured and its service listings be moved to another machine.

subtitle: Programming interfaces and file formats that let an application find and register network services the same way on every system.

tldr.problem: Applications that want to find a network service have no standard way to do it. Each product invents its own interface, and a service that cannot be rewritten cannot advertise itself at all.
tldr.mechanism: The memo defines an API for the Service Location Protocol in C and Java, plus two portable file formats: one for configuration and one for service registrations that can be moved between systems.
tldr.outcome: The memo is Informational and defines no protocol. It gives programmers a common set of calls for registering services and searching for them, so that an application written against the API can move between implementations without being rewritten.

today: RFC 2614 is an Informational memo from June 1999 and has not been obsoleted or updated. It defines a programming interface and two file formats rather than a protocol; the protocol it wraps, Service Location Protocol version 2, is specified in RFC 2608.

sections.title: What the API Is For
sections.content:
The Service Location Protocol (SLP) provides a way for clients to discover network services dynamically. With SLP it is simple to offer highly available services that require no user configuration or assistance from network administrators prior to use.

This memo describes standardized APIs for SLP in C and Java, together with standardized formats for configuration files and for serialized registration files. The APIs are modular and are designed to allow implementations to offer just the feature set needed. The file formats let SLP agents set network and other parameters in a portable way. The serialized file format allows legacy services to be registered with SLP directory agents in cases where modifying the legacy service program code is difficult or impossible, and it allows a registration database to be exchanged portably.

The overall goal of the API is to enable source portability of applications that use it between different implementations of SLP. The result should facilitate the adoption of SLP and the conversion of clients and service programs to SLP.

The goals differ between the two bindings. The goals of the C binding are to create a minimal but complete access to the functionality of the SLP protocol, allowing for simple memory management and limited code size. The Java API provides for modular implementations, where unneeded features can be omitted, and an object oriented interface to the complete set of SLP data and functionality. The standardized configuration file and serialized file formats provide a simple syntax with complete functional coverage of the protocol, but without system dependent properties and secure information.
sections.plainLanguage: The point of the interface is that the same program should work on any system that has the Service Location Protocol installed, so an application does not have to be rewritten for each supplier's implementation. The C version is deliberately small and simple to implement. The Java version is an object model where a program can leave out the parts it does not need.

sections.title: Agents, Services, Scopes and Service Types
sections.content:
Three kinds of process make up the framework.

  • A Service Agent (SA) is the Service Location process or library that allows service software to register and deregister itself with the SLP framework. Service agents respond to user agent service requests, detect directory agents, and register service advertisements with them.
  • A User Agent (UA) is the Service Location process or library that allows SLP requests to be made on behalf of a client process. User agents automatically direct requests to directory agents when they exist, and in their absence they make requests to service agents.
  • A Directory Agent (DA) is a service that automatically gathers service advertisements from service agents in order to provide them to user agents.

Many operating system platforms allow only a single process to listen on a particular port number, and service agents are required to listen on a multicast address. Implementations on such platforms that want to support multiple service agents on one machine need a single process to do the listening while the advertising service agents communicate with it through another mechanism. That single listening process is called an SA server. SA servers share many characteristics with directory agents but are not the same thing.

A service advertisement is a URL, possibly combined with service attributes, made available to user agents by service agents either directly or via a directory agent. A service of a particular type announces its availability with a service: URL, which includes its service access point, meaning the domain name or IP address and possibly its port number, and optionally basic configuration parameters. The syntax of the service: URL is defined in the service template, a document that describes the URL syntax for a given service type and defines all the service attributes for that type, including their meaning, their defaults and the constraints on the values they may take. The values that can be assigned to service attributes are also defined by the template.

Two further terms control who sees what. A scope is a string used to control the availability of service advertisements. Every SLP agent is configured with one or more scope strings. Scopes are assigned by site administrators to group services for many purposes, but chiefly as a means of scalability: directory agents store only services advertised with a scope string matching the scopes they are configured with. A naming authority is a suffix to the service type string that completely changes the meaning of the service type. Naming authorities are used for private definitions of well known service types and for experimental service type extensions. The default naming authority is IANA, which must not be explicitly included; service types with the IANA naming authority are registered with the Internet Assigned Numbers Authority.
sections.plainLanguage: Three roles appear. The service agent belongs to the program offering the service and registers it. The user agent belongs to the program looking for a service and asks on its behalf. The directory agent is a cache in between: it collects what has been advertised so that lookups do not have to reach every machine. A scope is a label that keeps services apart, so a large site only hears about the services it cares about.

sections.title: Configuration and Registration File Formats
sections.content:
Both file formats are defined in the UTF-8 character set. Attribute tags and values in the serialized registration file require the SLP reserved characters to be escaped: the characters (, ), ,, \, !, <, =, > and ~, together with control characters below 0x0020 and the character 0x007f. The escapes are formed exactly as for the wire protocol, a backslash followed by two hex digits representing the character, so the escape for a comma is \2c. The characters newline, carriage return, tab and underscore are prohibited from attribute tags by the SLP wire syntax grammar.

The configuration file format is a newline delimited list of zero or more property definitions. Each property definition corresponds to a particular configurable SLP, network or other parameter in one or more of the three SLP agents. The grammar is given in ABNF, and the file is written as lines of the form tag = value-list, with comment lines introduced by a hash or a semicolon character.

With the exception of net.slp.useScopes, net.slp.DAAddresses and net.slp.isBroadcastOnly, all other properties can be changed through the property accessors in the C and Java APIs. Those accessors change the values in the running agent program and do not affect the values in the configuration file. The three exceptions are read-only for stated reasons: the scopes and the directory agent addresses control the agent's view of the world and are therefore critical to the scope discovery algorithm, and whether the local network uses broadcast or multicast is not likely to change during the course of the program's execution, so changing it might invalidate the networking configuration.

The serialized registration file contains a group of registrations that a directory agent or SA server registers when it starts up. These registrations are primarily for older service programs that do not internally support SLP and cannot be converted, and for portably exchanging registrations between SLP implementations. Each registration carries a URL, a language tag, a lifetime and optionally a service type, a scope list and a list of attributes. If the maximum lifetime is specified, 65535 seconds, the registration is taken to be permanent and is continually refreshed by the agent until it exits. If the scope list contains scopes that are not in the agent's configured scopes, the library should reject the registration and issue a warning.

The memo also covers multihomed machines, where the bandwidth and latency of different interfaces differ enough to need separate settings. The net.slp.interfaces property lists the SLP enabled interfaces, and an implementation may allow a property to be set per interface by appending the interface address to the property name. The memo warns that the property must only be set if there is no routing between the interfaces, and that even where unicast packets are not routed, multicast may be routed through another router, in which case listening on several interfaces can make the agent answer the same request twice with different addresses.
sections.plainLanguage: The configuration file is a list of settings, one per line, that says how an agent should behave: which addresses to use, which scopes to work in, whether to act as a directory agent, and so on. The registration file is a list of services, and it exists so that a service which cannot be rewritten can still be listed, and so that a list of services can be moved from one machine to another.

sections.title: The Protocol API in C
sections.content:
The C binding opens an SLPHandle with SLPOpen and closes it with SLPClose. The handle carries the language locale in which registrations and requests are made. The core protocol calls are these.

  • SLPReg registers the URL in pcSrvURL with the lifetime usLifetime and the attribute list in pcAttrs. The lifetime must be nonzero and no greater than SLP_LIFETIME_MAXIMUM. A fresh flag says whether the registration is new, in which case it replaces any existing registrations, or an update of an existing one. The attribute list is a comma separated list of attribute assignments in the wire format, including escaping of reserved characters, and the empty string means no attributes. The library is required to perform the operation in all scopes obtained through configuration.
  • SLPDereg removes a registration, and SLPDelAttrs removes attributes from one.
  • SLPFindSrvTypes lists the service types available in one or more scopes, calling a callback for each type found.
  • SLPFindSrvs lists the services of a given type, calling a callback for each URL.
  • SLPFindAttrs lists the attributes of a given service type.

Several miscellaneous functions complete the API. SLPGetRefreshInterval returns the maximum across all directory agents of the minimum refresh interval, so that a service agent which uses it will not have a refresh rejected. SLPFindScopes finds the scopes in use. SLPParseSrvURL breaks a service URL into its parts. SLPEscape and SLPUnescape handle the reserved characters. SLPFree releases memory returned by the API. SLPGetProperty and SLPSetProperty read and write configuration properties.

Results can be returned synchronously or asynchronously. In the asynchronous form the API calls a callback for each result as it arrives, and an error during correspondence with a particular remote agent is reported through the first callback after the error occurs, which would normally carry the results of the correspondence. This lets the calling code decide whether the operation should be terminated or continue. Some errors are fatal, such as a parse error, and in those cases the API library terminates the operation. Callbacks are not permitted to call back into the API on the same handle, directly or indirectly; an attempt to do so returns an error.

The error codes are the same in both bindings, although each language returns them in its own way. Codes reported by a remote agent are LANGUAGE_NOT_SUPPORTED, PARSE_ERROR, INVALID_REGISTRATION, AUTHENTICATION_ABSENT and INVALID_UPDATE. Codes that result from interactions with remote agents or can occur locally are AUTHENTICATION_FAILED, SCOPE_NOT_SUPPORTED and REFRESH_REJECTED. Codes generated by a program interacting with the API, which do not involve a remote agent, are NOT_IMPLEMENTED, NETWORK_INIT_FAILED, NETWORK_TIMED_OUT, NETWORK_ERROR, BUFFER_OVERFLOW, MEMORY_ALLOC_FAILED, PARAMETER_BAD, INTERNAL_SYSTEM_ERROR, HANDLE_IN_USE and TYPE_ERROR.
sections.plainLanguage: A program opens a handle, registers its service with an address and a lifetime, and then asks for the services or service types it wants. Results can come back one at a time through a callback, so a long search does not have to wait for everything. Failures are reported with named error codes, most of which come from a remote agent and a few of which are local problems such as a bad parameter or a network that would not start.

sections.title: The Java Binding
sections.content:
The Java API models the various SLP entities in classes and objects. The ServiceLocationManager class contains methods that return instances of objects implementing service agent and user agent capability, each modelled in an interface: the Locator interface provides user agent capability and the Advertiser interface provides service agent capability. The abstract class TemplateRegistry contains methods that return objects for template introspection and attribute type checking, and a concrete subclass instance of it is returned by a class method. The ServiceURL, ServiceType and ServiceLocationAttribute classes model the basic SLP concepts.

All SLP classes and interfaces are located within a single package. The package name should begin with the name of the implementation and conclude with the suffix slp, so a hypothetical implementation from the University of Michigan would use edu.umich.slp. This follows the Java convention of prepending the top level DNS domain name of the organisation implementing the package onto the organisation's name.

Java handles errors differently from C. Most parameters to API methods are required to be non-null, and when parameters are checked for validity or their syntax is checked, the API throws IllegalArgumentException, a subclass of RuntimeException which is unchecked by the compiler, so clients are reminded to include try and catch blocks for it where the relevant parameters could be erroneous. Standard Java practice would encode every exceptional condition as a separate subclass of Exception, but because of the relatively high cost in code size of Exception subclasses, the API contains only a single Exception subclass with the different conditions determined by an integer error code property. That class is ServiceLocationException, and a subset of the error codes, appropriate to Java, is available as constants on it. The subset excludes error codes such as MEMORY_ALLOC_FAILED.

The Java binding carries its own implementation notes on refreshing registrations, parsing alternate transports in a service URL, string attribute values, client side syntax checking, language locale handling, setting SLP system properties, multithreading, modular implementations and asynchronous and incremental return semantics.
sections.plainLanguage: The Java version is built around classes: one class hands out the objects that advertise services and the objects that look for them, and other classes hold the pieces of a service such as its URL, its type and its attributes. Errors are reported through a single exception class with a numeric code, because Java exception classes are expensive in code size.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Security is handled within the API library and is not exposed to API clients except in the form of exceptions. The net.slp.securityEnabled property determines whether a service agent client's messages are signed, but a user agent client should be prepared for an authentication exception at any time, because it may contact a directory agent with authenticated advertisements.

The memo spells out the threat. An adversary could delete valid service advertisements, provide false service information, and deny user agents knowledge of existing services, unless the mechanisms in SLP for authenticating SLP messages are used. Those mechanisms allow DAAdverts, SAAdverts, service URLs and service attributes to be verified using digital cryptography. For this reason, all SLP agents should be configured to use SLP SPIs.
sections.plainLanguage: Someone on the network could remove advertisements, invent false ones, or hide real services from the programs that look for them. SLP has a mechanism for signing messages so that a receiver can check where an advertisement came from, and the memo says every agent should be set up to use it. The library handles the signing itself, so the program using the API only has to cope with an exception if a check fails.

viz.caption: THE CONFIGURATION FILE GRAMMAR, AS GIVEN IN RFC 2614

data.title: Configuration file ABNF
data.code:
config-file   =  line-list
line-list     =  line / line line-list
line          =  property-line / comment-line
comment-line  =  ( "#" / ";" ) 1*allchar newline
property-line =  property newline
property      =  tag "=" value-list
tag           =  prop / prop "." tag
prop          =  1*tagchar
value-list    =  value / value "," value-list
value         =  int / bool / "(" value-list ")" / string
int           =  1*DIGIT
bool          =  "true" / "false" / "TRUE" / "FALSE"
newline       =  CR / ( CRLF )
string        =  1*stringchar
